items.body: Our third iteration of the " Sculpting Silence " series, brings us to France, for a trio with Alexandra Grimal on saxophones, voice, harmonium, nōkan, shakuhachi, Naoto Yamagishi on percussions and Alexandre Saada on piano and harmonium. The title, Marée Basse , is French for “low tide”: the moment when the sea withdraws, leaving behind a wide, empty stretch of beach scattered with shells, tiny creatures, and fragments the waves have carried ashore. The music evokes much the same landscape. It takes this open space for granted, allowing the notes of saxophone, piano, and percussion to appear sparsely, sometimes only for brief moments before disappearing again. All three musicians are minimalists, deeply attentive to the overall sound yet reluctant to impose themselves upon it, as though the tones themselves should determine whether, and when, they wish to interact. Every sound feels tender and fragile, unobtrusive and gentle—and often completely absent. Silence is not merely the space between the notes; it is an essential part of the music itself. This is particularly striking in the thirty-minute second track, where, roughly halfway through, there is almost a full minute of near silence, with only faint crackling sounds barely audible in the background. When the music gradually returns, the instrumentation has subtly shifted: the harmonium introduces a handful of sustained tones, joined by Grimal's wordless singing, equally elongated and sensitive. Towards the end of the piece, the sound becomes fuller and more agitated, as though a sudden gust of wind were stirring the waves and awakening the distant cries of seagulls. Once again, silence plays an essential role in this music, much as it does in Japanese art, which has fascinated Grimaldi in recent years. Here, absence is not a lack but a presence of its own—a space in which the smallest sounds can emerge, linger for a moment, and then quietly disappear. Enjoy! Listen and download from Bandcamp . items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以'低潮'为意象，构建了一片声音退场后裸露的海滩景观。三位音乐家以极度克制的极简主义姿态，让萨克斯、钢琴与打击乐稀疏出现，每一声都脆弱而短暂。在长达三十分钟的第二轨中，音乐在近一分钟的近乎沉默后缓缓回归，簧风琴引入持续长音，Grimal的无词哼唱与其交织，尾声处音色骤然丰沛，如海风骤起。沉默本身被作为乐音的延伸来对待，留白中诞生的微小声响成为结构的核心。Grimal近年对日本艺术的迷恋在此显现——缺席并非匮乏，而是一种独立的在场，为最细微的声音留出显现、停留、消散的空间。专辑融合日本传统乐器（能管、尺八）与西方即兴传统，呈现出罕见的跨文化静默美学。

items.body: Photo by Vins Pedrata. Courtesy the artist Sven Fritz is an artist from Germany, who has various ongoing projects that explore performance, experimental music, and sound art. We had the chance to converse over email about his latest work, Der Saal tobt, realized under the Ervin Omsk moniker, published by Orange Milk. The interview was edited collaboratively with the artist. David Murrieta Flores (ACL): Hi Sven, could you please talk a bit about the Ervin Omsk project for readers who are unfamiliar with it? Sven Fritz (EO): Hi David, sure. Ervin Omsk is a pseudonym I’ve been using to release experimental electronic music since 2020. The name doesn’t actually have any special meaning; it’s simply an anagram of my two first names. The project began in 2018 with a few musical collages that were strongly connected to the idea of exploring an abstract painting or sculpture in a particular room—in other words, a very spatial approach, in which I combined diverse sounds from a modular system, field recordings, voice, and so on. Fortunately, Orange Milk was willing to release these tracks on tape in 2020, with artwork by Keith Rankin. In 2023, a second album, titled Schmalster Point, was released on vinyl, with artwork by Brenna Murphy. Now the third album, Der Saal tobt, is being released on tape and CD, with artwork by Lukas Schmenger. Ervin Omsk is currently one of several projects I’m working on. However, it’s the only solo project, and therefore also the most intense one. All my other projects are collaborative—for example, most recently with the French musician Amédée de Murcia. Together, we released an album in March on the Italian label Søvn. There’s also the Hui project, which I’m doing together with Johannes Schebler (Baldruin). An album has just been released on Jollies, and another one was released on Nonlocal Research last year. I’m also part of the artist collective Trickster, where I collaborate with other artists to realize scenarios in the sense of a Gesamtkunstwerk. My role here often involves musical performances lasting several hours and spread out over multiple days. All of my projects fall within the realm of experimental electronic music, and Ervin Omsk really benefits from the many experiences I’ve had working with all these other musicians. This applies not only to production, but also to the concerts I play as Ervin Omsk. These performances, however, are more like interpretations or improvised versions of the tracks I release. ACL: As the liner notes describe it, Der Saal tobt is mimicry of an orchestral body. Usually, we would understand such a body as mechanically efficient and well-coordinated, tuned and built through practice. However, the album understands it differently, and the result is slightly opposite: it’s a body that seems “unpracticed”. How do you understand the relationships between these bodies’ organs? How do you understand the differences between the modern, “well-oiled” orchestra and the album’s version of it? EO: I recently went to a concert where a chamber ensemble performed a piece that really moved me. At the same time, I realized that I actually didn’t really know what was going on. I have no academic background in this field. For example, I lack knowledge of music history and theory, notation, instrumentology, the roles within an ensemble, and so on. So I can only form a vague idea of what is happening in this music. I sense its dissonance, complexity, and openness; at times, it almost feels improvised. At the same time, I associate orchestral music with something highbrow and inaccessible. And that would be, so to speak, a different perspective from the outside. I generally have a rather ambivalent relationship with high culture, because it often caters to unchanging expectations and cultivates a kind of institutional sophistication. And in this context, the terms “efficient” and “coordinated” become interesting: these are actually very performance-oriented categories, which I would spontaneously associate with economics and sport. What do they have to do with music? But yes, an orchestra also needs this high degree of functionality, because, for example, it follows an idea or an order in the form of a notation. The musicians ensure that everything runs smoothly because they have mastered their instruments. To put it bluntly, we could argue that a modern, well-oiled orchestra must function—which sounds almost a bit cold and predictable. In music or art, however, I am not interested in categories like “well rehearsed,” “efficient,” and “coordinated” at first. It is rather the state outside these functions that moves me. To me, the intuitive and the seemingly contradictory have always been special qualities. There is, for example, that brief moment when an orchestra or a small ensemble tunes up. It is an undefined jumble of sounds, a wonderful moment of uncertainty. I am fascinated by the orchestra pit and its sound. But I come from a different musical background, both technically and culturally. I only play guitar, I can sing, and I know some things about synths and computer music. So I can’t imitate the orchestra; I can only bring electronic instruments into play, which then, through practice, become their own form of an orchestral body. And the interactions between the organs aren’t without tension; they sometimes get in each other’s way, and they don’t always speak the same language. And that’s what makes their relationships so special to me. There’s no oil here—more like sand in the gears and friction, to stick with your analogy. ACL: What is the process that you follow in order to craft a track? How do you understand the connections between tracks, once they are finished? EO: I can hardly describe it, really. There is no linear or additive process: each track is the result of countless intuitive decisions, right down to the smallest moments. I’m obsessed with details. The computer of course offers infinite possibilities and an overwhelming freedom. But that also means I usually can’t remember how the individual tracks were made. But I’ll try to describe it using the last track on the album as an example—which was actually the first track I produced: Right at the beginning, I made some very simple and short recordings of an alto recorder that I had borrowed from a friend and musician. After sampling and processing these recordings, the flute’s physical qualities were still there—the airiness, the directness, the softness, the hiss, and so on—but I could tune it freely and also control its overtones and noise, among other things. In fact, it suddenly seemed more like a symbol for an entire group of woodwind instruments or like an instrument that wanted to be several at once. And yet it still had something artificial about it. This impression was reinforced by the way it was played. Arpeggiators, whose tempo and rate were modulated by LFOs; animated envelopes that made glissandos possible; and the layering of several abstract flutes at once, varying only in their playing and sound. Then combined and blended with noises and glitches that picked up on the flutes’ patterns and intonations, countered them, and made them seem alien. Then it got a bit crowded, maybe like rush hour at the main train station. So then it was a constant process of sorting, resampling, stretching, compressing, cutting, copying, pasting, deleting, and leaving pauses—until the track was finished. Something like that, very roughly. And as I said, there’s no single process that applies equally to all tracks. Other tracks have undergone several transformations. They were actually finished; then I completely rearranged them in the context of the entire album, because they didn’t feel right within the album’s dynamic, and the sequence of the tracks that unfolds over just 27 minutes. In addition, on this album I deliberately used certain sounds—such as the processed alto recorder— in several tracks, either obviously or just as a trace. And then, for me, all the pieces take place in the same space; they’re close and direct. Photo of Trickster setup by Sven Fritz. Courtesy the artist. ACL: What sort of gear do you use in this process? Thinking of gear less in terms of straightforward tools, and more socially in terms of extensions of your own thoughts and body, what does all this gear allow you to do? What does it inhibit you from doing? EO: I always try not to own too much gear. Even in production, I use only a few very specific and experimental tools so as not to unnecessarily expand the range of possibilities: a small modular system, MIDI controllers, Ableton Live, with digital samplers, sound generators, M4L devices, a few effects, and then a few flutes and microphones. I like the second part of your question. As a child, I played a home organ—two manuals, bass pedals. After that, I played electric guitar and sang for a long time, always in the context of bands. Vocals and guitar, in particular, are two very direct and physical instruments. It’s almost impossible to transfer that feeling to the world of synthesizers and computers, because playing them is less about gestures and more about fine motor skills involving the hands, fingers, eyes and ears: knobs, pads, trackpads, clicking, looking, listening and so on. But when it comes to abstract thinking about music, synthesizers and computers offer another advantage. They expand the scope of what I can imagine musically and put me in a constant state of learning and wonder. It’s sometimes like a rush. Surely also because I don’t understand everything. But in any case, it changes my own perception of sound, because these machines basically function like auditory microscopes. You can dive incredibly deep with your ears and your thoughts. ACL: Going back to the idea of orchestration, do you understand yourself as the orchestra’s director? Perhaps the orchestra itself, as an abstract embodiment? Perhaps the orchestra’s prompt-maker, to use contemporary code? In short – what is your own position within or without the orchestral body of the album? EO: A prompt-maker relies on clear codes or language as commands, right? That wouldn’t be immediate enough. And unfortunately, I don’t know much about the work of a conductor. But if I may set that aside for a moment, it might be something between a conductor and the orchestra itself. Here’s how I picture it: there’s a room full of objects, no musicians. So I rush through the ranks and set these objects into motion, sound, gestures, and relationships with one another. That would be very closely linked to experiences with live performances—both the role of the conductor and the abstract embodiment. Two examples: There’s this collective project called Trickster, which I’ve already mentioned: very irregularly, we realize a series of evenings as an image—no hierarchy, no stage, no beginning, no end, and thus no mood-setting service. In one of the those projects, I arranged 6–8 different speakers, several mixers, an electric guitar, a spontaneous choir of friends, several synthesizers, a percussionist, and two friends playing the French horn and the soprano recorder, spread throughout a room of about 100 square meters. Here, my role was more like that of a conductor who, over the course of about five hours, activated and collaged all of this using clear impulses and several loopers. Charging and discharging the space, playfully and improvisationally. Then recently I put together a live setup for some shows that had to fit into a backpack. A computer, two MIDI controllers, a small semi-modular synthesizer, and a microphone for vocals. Yet I prepared it in such a way that there were always five different instruments that I could play simultaneously. That was a bit demanding, but very direct, all on a small table—more as if I were many instruments, or, if you will, the orchestra itself. Turning knobs, playing pads, plugging in cables, tuning, singing, applying effects, controlling, not controlling. Photo by Matt Favero. Courtesy the artist. ACL: I’d like to return now to the question of mimicry – it’s an aesthetically loaded term, but it’s possible to contrast it with the idea that there is something organic to the body we are listening to in the album. If we understand the album’s body as more of an automaton, what are its possibilities/capacities/abilities when thinking about traditional musical categories of representation like “expression”? EO: Oh, that’s a really tough question, and I’m not sure I fully understand it. Mechanization could also be understood as a rigid and hierarchical process, but the automaton of the album feels alive to me. That would be more like a cyborg, right? But sure, let’s stick with the image of the automaton. I don’t think of it as a concrete thing with a particular physical form, but rather as an abstract machine, as algorithms and processes. In order to see what abilities it has in terms of traditional musical categories, I have to listen to it. So I’ll pretend for a moment that I didn’t build the automaton. At first, it sounds to me like a machine that seems to define its own form, processes, and movements, acrobatic and unpredictable, like a shapeshifter. It leads an inscrutable life of its own. The mistakes it makes are constantly incorporated into its search for form. A complex and delicate act. But only on the first, and perhaps the second, listening. Once you have become familiar with the complexity, the mechanisms, and the glitches, the form and nature of the automaton become clearer. Perhaps that is the moment when we can return to the “category of representation,” once we have understood the language of the automaton. Because “musical expression” may not be as organic, immediate, and human as we like to think. It is also part of a tradition and works through codes, conventions, expectations, and learned gestures—only seemingly self-evident. The automaton, of course, is only indirectly part of this tradition. In this logic, perhaps the ability of the automaton does not lie in “expressing” something in the classical sense, but in using, shifting, exaggerating, or also refusing these codes of expression. It maybe has the potential to transform many different sounds, instruments, gestures, figures, and experiments into a different but nevertheless familiar form of expression. And perhaps through its artificiality and distance it can make something audible that a human body would not do in this way. But the question really is very abstract. I hope I was able to give a somewhat meaningful answer here. Photo by Tobias Ullrich. Courtesy the artist. ACL: You did, thank you! Now, I’m interested in the meaning of the various track titles. There’s a playful overtone about things going wrong, failing in wholesome ways, or simply being the result of an essay in something (the “Memo Grisaille”, for instance, which alludes to the formative, practical painting made in shades of black or grey that emerged in the Renaissance). What links the process through which you made each track with the titles you chose for them? EO: Collecting titles or sentences is an independent process that I and other friends have been practicing since art school. I’m interested in titles because they add an associative layer to the individual track or the entire album. The album artwork by Lukas Schmenger does that too, by the way. Like the artwork, the titles are an important part of the album, even though they only come into the process at a later stage. I think the titles of the album relate in a certain way to its dynamics and moods. So I really associate the album title “Der Saal tobt” with an image of an agitated and unrestrained group of people. A feeling and sound somewhere between threat and excitement maybe. At the same time, it’s important for me to break up some kind of sonic overload with an everyday and blunt remark like “Beim besten Willen,” which rather expresses a refusal or incomprehension. So I also like the laconic quality of titles. With “Memo Grisaille,” though, it wasn’t my intention to trivialize this art-historical term. I simply like the combination of the words in terms of their sound, and the piece has something fragile and searching about it, like a memory that only becomes sharp and distinct in certain moments. So, with each title, there is an association that relates to the mood of the piece—with it or against it. ACL: Your previous album already explored a sense of joy derived from electronic sound interactions. Considering the track title themes, I think the argument can be made that there’s a humorous undercurrent in Der Saal tobt – there’s a philosophical perspective that says, basically, that it’s funny when things act like persons, but also the other way around. As the album’s automaton furiously fumbles around, we could be inspired to laugh: have you ever thought of experimental electronic music as possibly funny? Would you see a role for humor within your work, in the past, now, and in the future? EO: Experimental electronic music can be fun, sure. But so far, I haven’t gotten that feeling from this album. Then again, maybe I’m just missing something because I wasn’t sitting at the instruments or in front of the computer laughing while making it. Maybe it’s already fun when something unexpected happens. The staging of errors that make the automaton seem human, the unusual sounds, the friction in the gears, getting tangled up in the gestures—all of that could be interpreted as fun. For me, these are necessities, because I fear a well-oiled machine—and thus the predictable. And perhaps also I can’t take things, or myself, too seriously. So there may, after all, be a certain humorous distance, and therefore an unconscious influence on the tracks. But as the author myself, I can’t hear it. And that means humor would not have a defined role right now. If anything, it just happens, as it does in encounters with other people. For me, humor is indispensable there. In any case, I want to keep thinking about your question. There are quite a few inspiring examples in music, but also in visual art, that I would definitely describe as humorous. And maybe humor can get a more definite role in my work too. ACL: Thank you very much for your time, Sven. Is there anything else you’d like to tell our readers before closing this interview? EO: I’d like to thank you for these really challenging and intense questions. They went quite deep, and I found it very inspiring to think about them. Now I’m curious to know what it’s like to listen to the album after reading this interview—how it affects the way we perceive and contextualize this music. Especially since the album doesn’t necessarily need a strong conceptual framework, as it was created largely intuitively. Talking about it this way now almost feels like a kind of mental post-production, even though the music is already finished. And I consider it something special in itself to be able to release music like this, in the hope that there will be a few people out there who will actually listen to it and perhaps even find something in it. Thanks again for this opportunity.

items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评以访谈形式呈现，聚焦德国艺术家Sven Fritz的Ervin Omsk项目及其第三张专辑《Der Saal tobt》。Ervin Omsk自2020年起以化名发表实验电子音乐，其创作源于对特定空间中抽象绘画与雕塑的听觉转译，融合模块化系统、现场录音与人声等多源素材，构建出空间感强烈的声音拼贴。新作概念是对管弦乐体的模拟，却刻意呈现一种未经排练的、笨拙的群体状态，与精密协调的传统乐团形成对照。Orange Milk等独立厂牌的发行脉络、Keith Rankin、Brenna Murphy等视觉艺术家的封面合作，以及艺术家同时参与的多项合作计划（包括与法国音乐人、与Baldruin的Hui项目、以及Trickster集体），共同勾勒出一个扎根于地下实验场景、强调跨媒介与长期协作的创作生态。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Contrasts define Aria for Labellum Tongues, the third album from the Houston, Texas-based band Kraanerg. From the opening track, "Amargosa Raga," the distorted guitar seems to clash with the violin, which follows its own distinct musical path, creating a unique sound. The band goes beyond the experiments of the Electric Light Orchestra, taking those ideas further by playing with atonality and, even better, finding a rhythm that makes perfect sense within that exploration. For amidst that chaos and rawness (qualities that are also classical in nature) there is genuine feeling.There is something hypnotic about the title track: the vocals, the band's frenetic rhythm, and Nat Bergrin's plaintive singing, accompanied by the violin and later turning operatic, evoke the most avant-garde side of Tom Waits. It suggests a cabaret where Fellini and Marc Ribot might coexist, yet it also feels as if the Mahavishnu Orchestra had gone punk.In "Blessings in Silk, Saffron, and Naran-Ji," the impression persists of hearing a classic piano-and-violin duo fused with a visceral rock band. When the saxophones join in and Nat Bergrin begins to croon, moving beyond the piano's traditional role, she makes another fundamental contribution, embodying through her voice that apparent contradiction between refinement and rawness, order and chaos, light and shadow. Maximilian Jacobs's violin evokes the classical style of cellist Erik Friedlander or the Balanescu Quartet, yet within a rock context, it takes on a weight that is more dramatic, more "pathetic" in the classical sense, grounded by Bergrin's earthy vocals.Anguloa Virginalis ("A Woman's Face") is a reinterpretation of jazz sensibility filtered through a personal lens, where the vibraphone provides the perfect touch. Then, Iron Sign of the Masdevallia begins, almost like a ritual, where, amidst wind and string arrangements as elaborate, complex, and sophisticated as Dan Britton's contemporary music, the spirit of John Zorn and a raw, rugged sound slip in, crossing a slender "Canterbury" bridge. And there are pieces of undeniable beauty and delicate craftsmanship that, underpinned by the solid foundation of drums and bass, take on a different texture. For the result is an orchestra of dark times, where the symphonic quality found within is progressive in a unique way.As with Dan Britton, the vocals aren't a strong point, but Kraanerg turns this into a virtue, treating the voice as just another dissonant instrument that contributes to the unique balance they aim for... and achieve. "Visible to the Wrong Faces" marks a return to twenty-minute suites, opening with piano and the band's signature bass synthesizer. A viola and a second guitar join in a crescendo, adding depth and lower-register resonance; syncopated, Eastern-influenced rhythms then take hold, while the violin and vibraphone toy with a near-pop melody that shifts tempo as Nat hums along, and a touch of Zappa creeps in, specifically the "cosmic sound" variety. The finale becomes epic, conjuring up even more unusual sonic fusions, a strange kind of epic where Gong and Renaissance might share the studio. Kraanerg offers a sensory experience that remains unaffected by time, as it unfolds outside of it.

items._cn_summary: Kraanerg 来自美国休斯顿，这张专辑以对比为核心美学，扭曲吉他与小提琴各自遵循不同的音乐路径，形成独特的声响张力。乐队将无调性探索与节奏感融合，在混沌与原始中注入真挚情感。标题曲充满催眠效果，人声与狂躁节奏营造出Tom Waits式的前卫氛围，融合Fellini式的卡巴莱剧场感与朋克化的Mahavishnu Orchestra想象。钢琴与小提琴二重奏与摇滚乐队的结合贯穿始终，颤音琴的爵士触感、东方影响的切分节奏、Zappa式的怪诞旋律以及Zorn式粗砺质感相互交织。乐队将人声视为另一件不和谐乐器，刻意削弱其传统旋律功能，使其融入整体的实验平衡中。作为当代作曲与前卫摇滚的跨界产物，专辑在交响性框架内构建出黑暗时代的管弦乐幻境。

items.body: On " Chant ", another sculptor of silence shows her art. The magician is Magda Mayas, whose explorations of the outside and inside of her piano keeps astonishing us, including her inventiveness to create unheard sounds. Mayas is not only a musician, but also an academic researcher with several publications to her name, getting her PhD on the subject of " Orchestrating Timbre – Unfolding Processes of Timbre and Memory in Improvisational Piano Performance" (2019/20), which examines improvisation through timbre, space, movement, objects, and listening. I'm adding a few videos here to show her art. The first is an exercise that Magda Mayas developed for the Hochschule Luzern called " Thinking Silent Matter ". The excercise focuses on improvisation in a large ensemble context, bringing attention to silence and reduced sound material with slowly changing parameters, starting with the relevant quote : "... silence not only as absence of sound, but also silence as part of the sound" . In the video she guides her students through the concept of the exercise. Indeed, silence matters. It is even essential to anything we hear, whether we are aware of it or not, so why not actively use it in music? On the tree pieces of the album, she shows this in very different formats. The first and last piece were recorded in Australia, with two years apart, the middle track was recorded in Berlin in Tony Buck's Brief Sand Studio. The opening track, “ Embodied ,” recorded live at the SoundOut Festival in Canberra in February 2025, establishes its language through restraint. The piano notes arrive slowly, and the silences between them are as significant as the sounds themselves. Rather than functioning as a conventional prelude, however, this spaciousness becomes the central compositional device. Against the sparse piano framework, elusive sounds emerge from objects and tools used to activate the strings, producing a shifting field of resonance whose sources remain deliberately indistinct. The music is notably sparse, but never static; its intensity lies in the sustained concentration with which each sound occupies the space. “ Halcyon ” extends this approach while pushing the sonic material into considerably harsher territory. Carefully paced piano chords are subjected to feedback from a guitar amplifier, alongside a guitar pickup and various other objects. The amplification and feedback transform the piano’s familiar timbre, extending each chord into a dense, sustained resonance. Despite the expanded textural palette, the harmonic language remains remarkably focused: pitches occupy a restricted register and coalesce around a clear tonal centre. This tension between harmonic simplicity and increasingly abrasive resonance gives the piece its mesmerising quality. Developed in 2023 during the Harringtons Lane artist residency in New South Wales, “ Chant ” approaches the piano from yet another angle. The piece’s playback was recorded on sixteen different pianos, foregrounding variations in tuning and the subtle differences between instruments. Its structure is deceptively simple, built around the quiet repetition of two chords whose minute variations in tuning and timbre continually alter their perceptual weight. The effect is both soothing and strangely intense. Through repetition, small shifts become magnified, turning what might initially appear static into something constantly in flux. Across these three works, there is a consistent interest in reducing musical materials to their essentials while expanding the possibilities of resonance, texture and perception. The music derives much of its power from this paradox: the means are often minimal, yet the listening experience is anything but. What emerges is an aesthetic that feels simultaneously rigorous and intuitive—fresh, inventive and deeply attentive to the physical properties of sound. The title piece was also performed by Mayas at Roulette, streamed live on 30 Apr 2024. The video gives a great insight in her music but also on the added ingredients in the interior of her piano, things you can assume when you see a concert, but can usually at best only guess at. Enjoy! Listen and download from Bandcamp . Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由钢琴家Magda Mayas创作，属于Unsounds厂牌发起的'Sculpting Silence'系列第四作。Mayas不仅是即兴音乐家，还拥有以音色、记忆与即兴钢琴演奏为题的博士学位。她的演奏大量利用钢琴内部物件、弦与放大器反馈，拓展传统钢琴的声响边界，将沉默本身视为声音材料的一部分。三首作品录制于不同地点与年份：开篇'Embodied'在堪培拉音乐节现场录音，以极度克制的钢琴音符与物件声响构建空旷的声场；'Halcyon'引入吉他放大器与拾音器反馈，在和声简洁与音色粗粝之间形成张力；同名曲'Chant'以十六架不同钢琴的录音叠合而成。她强调声音与空间、动作、聆听之间的关系，将声音的物质性作为即兴创作的核心方法。

items.body: Actress Radical Frame Making his return to the Ninja Tune label, Darren Cunningham practices typical elusiveness with doleful piano stabs amidst pounding surf and ambient textures Radical Frame by Actress Try to recall an Actress track and you won’t bring a melody or rhythm back. You’ll find only a noir sensation, the faint memory of wading through a city’s hazy silence at four in the morning, alone, but with something in the air around you that the skin registers before the mind does. A rusting Weltschmerz bleeds through Darren Cunningham’s music, dissolving evanescent motifs into lasting affect. Over twenty years into his career, Radical Frame sees the UK producer continue to explore music that resists forgetting. The almost preternatural allure of Cunningham’s first proper solo... The post Actress – Radical Frame appeared first on The Quietus.
items._cn_summary: Actress（本名Darren Cunningham）回归Ninja Tune厂牌，推出专辑《Radical Frame》。乐评指出他的音乐难以用旋律或节奏概括，而是营造一种凌晨四点独自穿行于城市雾霭中的黑色电影式氛围感知——一种通过皮肤而非头脑传递的感官印象。专辑在忧郁的钢琴短句、猛烈的噪音浪潮与绵延的氛围纹理之间穿行，将转瞬即逝的音乐动机溶解为持久的情感效应。乐评强调这是这位英国制作人二十余年职业生涯中持续探索的一种抵抗遗忘的音乐语言，延续了他早期独奏作品中对声音氛围近乎超自然般吸引力的追求，整体定位偏向实验电子与氛围音乐的交汇地带。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Recorded in London at Orange Recording Studios LTD. December 9-12, 1970 and then released early in 1971 by Global Records.A1. "Thursday Morning Sunrise" (11:38) not the opening I was expecting--ever--from a 1971 prog album much less a Jazz-Rock Fusion one. The deep, low, heavily distorted organ play sounds like Markus Pajakkala's baritone saxes and bass clarinet on his (memorable) 2017 Brutopianisti album! When other instruments finally join in they're all grotesquely distorted: Eberhard's wild (and virtuosic) electric bass, Siggi Schwab's Sonny-Sharrock/Arto Lindsay-like electric guitar, even the drumming/percussion work of Fred Braceful and Roland Wittich is wild. I wouldn't call this "Free Jazz" like something from Ornette Coleman, John Coltrane's post-A Love Supreme period, or Sun Ra's Arkestra, but a fusion of these with experimental sound explorations and, in the second half, the incorporation of sophisticated African rhythms with even some from the more avant-garde realms of Classical Music. I am blown away, incredibly impressed, and find myself incredibly entertained as well as fully enjoying this trail-blazing exercise in boundary-obliteration. Could this album have been a key food source for the inspiration of soon-to-appear bands like UNIVERS ZERO or AREA?--certainly this type of music (19.25/20)A2. "Lady Blue" (3:03) now, hearing this amazing song that combines Beatnik poetry-delivery musical formats with Classical Music choral traditions, I find myself asking whether or not Wolfgang, Eberhard, Siggi, and/or Fred were fans or progeny of George Russell's School of Esoteric Musics while George was a professor in residence at Sweden's Lund University. I absolutely love this! Another totally unexpected song that I find myself returning to over and over to try to fathom its creative scope. (9.75/10)A3. "Mellodroma 2a" (5:10) more choir appearances open this--from a distance--before Siggi's acoustic guitar enters playing with congas and double bass in what can only be descrived as a Folk Rock tune akin to something by Bert and John, The Pentangle, or The Incredible String Band. And the choir continues to make small appearances! These guys are amazing! The diverse interests and forms for their musical expression seems to have no bounds! Lite drums join in but it's the hand percussion that dominates with Eberhard's double bass Wonderful! Another song that totally took me by surprise and which lures me back again and again for repeated listens as I try desperately to fathom their thinking and desires. In the fourth minute there is a lull in which Siggi gets to show off a little more of his acoustic guitar skills, but then the rest of the band re-joins for a rousing finish with percussion and organ really bringing it (though no return of the choir). Wonderful! (9.333/10)B1. "Raga" (16:17) apparently Siggi Schwab had really gotten into a huge variety of World Music stringed instruments--and especially stringed instruments prevalent in India--like the but also zithers, psaltries, This track was actually written by Siggi, who is credited with a vast array of traditional, ethnic, and Indian stringed instruments on the record. Among the highly zither-like instruments he plays on the album and track are the swarmandal (credited as "surmandel") and the bulbul tarang. Siggi also contributed sitar, veena, tambura, and sarangi to the album's rich, psychedelic raga-rock sound. Eberhard, Fred, Roland, and Wolfgang do their best to provide inputs that they think will enhance, embellish, and not detract from Siggi's reverence for his Indian studies. I find the use of the full drum kit in the seventh through ninth minute to be a bit overwhelming and domineering to the Indian spirit being expressed but, it's a good awareness experiment and, fortunately, it ends so that the song can move into a new, more-percussion-centric passage--one that contains Eberhard's talking drum like bass play as well as a lot of intertwined and improvisationally-reactive percussion threads, gradually embellished by trumpet and, later, cymbal-crashing drum kit and distorted synth string sounds. Things quite down again in the sixteenth minute, leaving Siggi and his mates to finish the song with a thin palette of almost-incidental noises and percussives to usher Siggi's surmandel out. (By the way, Fred's drum play over this last sections is much more tasteful and respectful--much less invasive and brutal.) Another surreally-unexpected and eminently-enjoyable song that makes me wish I had been there--wish I could have been present for these practice and recording sessions as well as known these remarkably intrepid musicians! (28.25/30) B2. "Milkstreets" (4:15) a relatively unstructured melange of natural and unnatural (treated and electonic) sounds, many coming from African and Indian traditions. Interesting and historically significant (like the work of John Cage, Terry Riley, Herbie Hancock, Area and so many other adventurists). (8.875/10) Total time: 40:23YouTube provided me with three extra/bonus songs that apparently came from the same December 1970 London recording sessions but only saw the light of day (and a public awareness) on a 2008 CD release from the Long Hair label. They are also quite interesting and experimental, allowing for even more display of all the weird instruments that Siggi and Wolfgang had been playing around with. A/five stars; an absolute masterpiece of experimental and leading-edge Jazz-Rock Fusion. HIGHLY recommended and ESSENTIAL for any J-R Fusion and Progressive Rock fan.
items._cn_summary: 这张1971年发行的德国录音将爵士、前卫摇滚与实验声响探索熔于一炉。开场曲以深沉的失真管风琴与电贝斯构建出近乎工业感的音墙，融合自由爵士的即兴张力、非洲节奏与先锋古典音乐元素，呈现出强烈的边界消融意识。第二首短曲出人意料地将垮掉派诗歌朗诵与古典合唱传统结合，短小精悍却意蕴深远。第三首则转向民谣摇滚路线，加入原声吉他、康加鼓与合唱，展现乐队多元的音乐兴趣。最后的长篇作品聚焦世界音乐弦乐器的探索，延续实验精神。整体而言，乐队在爵士、前卫与世界音乐之间自由穿梭，手法大胆且富于冒险性，是欧洲前卫场景中不可忽视的声音档案。

items.body: What happens if the sun disappears? The question lingered over the stage at Viljandi Folk Festival on the morning its closing day. Tell Your Birds brought it there, playing songs from a still unreleased record in front of a crowd for the first time. Kristīne Tukre‘s concert kokle carried the melodies, Vija Moore‘s balafon sat under them, Kärt Tambet‘s bowed hiiu kannel cut across both, and everything the three of them played ran through Simone Spampinato‘s processing. They sang in Estonian and Latvian at once, each keeping the language they grew up speaking. Some of the material comes from those same traditions, chopped up and rebuilt inside the band’s own songs. The rest belongs to no repertoire at all, written on the chance that one day it might. Straight after the set, in the last hour before Tell Your Birds broke apart for the rest of the summer, we sat down with the four of them not far from the stage, with a temperamental recorder giving us a hard time and cutting out every few minutes. Our chat eventually fell into the band’s own working rhythm: a burst, a stop, a burst. Tukre and Spampinato live in Helsinki, Tambet in Viljandi, Moore in Riga. They get a few days together, write everything in that stretch, then go back to their own cities until the next one. In the hour before they scattered, they talked about where a tradition comes from and what you have to know before using it, about melodies written for a time that has not happened yet, and about the syllables that decide which language a song ends up in. Tell Your Birds started with a student project. All four met at the Sibelius Academy in Helsinki, in different departments, and Tambet dates the band from there: “We came together as a band back in 2023, but back then it was a very specific project. It was Vija [Moore], who is our percussionist, her bachelor concert project in Sibelius Academy in Finland, where we all studied together.” The concert called for soundscape music written for one place and recorded in it, and the place Moore picked was a forest near Ērgļi, a village in Latvia. They hauled the balafon, the percussion, the violin and the kokle out among the trees and played there, birds and insects carrying on around them and ending up on the tape along with everything else. For Spampinato that set the method for everything after it: “it was the first project where we all get together and thought, we recorded everything outside. We tried to record the instruments as they were part of the soundscape in that sense.” That turned into Pause in Nature, then Carry on with Hope, out on 1 November 2024. One year later they wanted more room to move, and Tambet marks autumn 2025 as the turn: “to write together and to think of music more widely, maybe not so specifically as we had done before“. Moore had been waiting for it: “I like that with this new music, we got to put it all together.” There was a lot to put together. The four met inside one institution and arrived there from four directions, and Moore starts with the two furthest from folk: “Simone comes from sound art, electronics, different sound design type of experience and worldview. And then Kristīne comes from a contemporary composition and contemporary kantele playing. Also, Kristīne is interested in baroque music.” She and Tambet are the two who came up in folk, she through percussion, Tambet through singing and the violin. The spread is the point for Moore: “Each of us have a different genre outlook. I think it all comes together in our music, and it’s very interesting.“ Tukre’s own route ran through the classical kantele, though her instrument at home is the kokle. The Estonian kannel, the Latvian kokle and the Finnish kantele are cousins in one family of box zithers, and the family resemblance is where it gets interesting for her: “We have a very interesting phenomenon here in the Baltics and in Finland. We have these string instruments; they’re similar, but at the same time very different. They have different names, but we, musicians, try to come together.” The players of all three look across the borders to each other’s instruments. She did exactly that, a kokle player going to Helsinki to learn the kantele at the Sibelius Academy: “That’s how I got to Finland. I got to meet Viia, Gert and Simone, and we started the band.“ Coming together now happens across three countries, which turns rehearsals and recording sessions into an exercise of dates, plans and travel tickets, so they work in blocks: several days in one of the three places, everything at once, then dispersal. For Moore the two halves stay separate: “We just intensively get into the music for those couple of days, and then go back to our real lives.” Where those blocks happen feeds the music too. “I also think us meeting for intensive times in different places has played a big role in the music. Because when we have come to Viljandi, we get to see into the Viljandi life, and we get to see into the whole Estonian culture, even social culture. It plays such a big role of explaining what a tradition means. And then also going to Latvia all together, that was the missing puzzle pieces.” Estonia, Latvia and Finland have all had their turn. Italy is still waiting, as Spampinato points out: “We have not been to Italy. What a terrible thing!” The residencies have gone further than rehearsal rooms and taken the four into each other’s family homes, which Moore counts as its own kind of source material: “In our residencies, it’s very nice that we’ve met each other’s families because families represent culture in a whole other coded way, it’s something not explainable by words.” What comes back from those weeks is a songbook the band builds itself. Tambet traces the bulk of it to the four of them: “Most of the music is actually original music that we have composed together, or separately, but brought it to this group.” Folk melodies feed into it, and so do myths, texts and lyrics that arrive as words alone. Before using any of it, Tambet wants the origin and the original purpose clear: “there’s a lot of using a tradition in music. You have to be aware of it, and translating it to others. It’s highly important that we’re aware where it’s coming from and what the original intention behind that tradition is, so we can translate it into our own musical language.” The traditions Spampinato grew up with are not the ones on the table. He comes from Sicily, but his folk roots lie in Ciociaria, a historical region of southern Lazio: “My folk background is actually from Ciociaria, not Sicilian.” What he brings instead comes from sound art, electronics and sound design, where the tradition is the sound itself: “My background is more about sound. What do we do with every little sound?” Put that question to folk music and you get the music he admires most: “I’m really a huge fan of experimental French folk music, Sourdure for example, and I think we are trying to get into that.” In practice it means cutting material up and putting it back together: “What we use a lot is chopping and sampling, this kind of collage, things colliding. Sometimes they’re all together, sometimes we really like the contrast.” The same goes for how the four handle it on stage, where the play is in the treatment, not the tunes: “Maybe the songs don’t seem that playful, but how we manage our material is super playful. Viia is playing with four mallets [on the balafon], I’m on the synth and then the guitar. It’s collage in that sense.“ The same collage habit carries into the lyrics, starting with language. Sometimes the four sing three languages at the same time, like a group chanting together, each in their own language instead of settling on a shared one. For Tukre, that’s the point: “We don’t make these language compromises.” The words themselves usually start from folk songs and folk tales, which she reworks before they can be sung now: “The language tends to be quite archaic and doesn’t always fit with the world we live in. So we like to shape it a little and add some reference points we can relate to, but keep the original idea our ancestors had in their folk songs.” The shaping mostly falls to her, in Spampinato’s words “the poet of the band“. A song’s meaning is often sketched in English first, but the language it ends up in is chosen by ear, and for Moore sound decides it: “We’re a lot based on the sound, so what sound are we searching for? That’s where the language plays a big role.” Syllable counts settle much of it: “Some songs require Estonian lyrics, you can just feel it fits better, and some songs are Latvian. The number of syllables each language uses for one word can be different, so we use that to our advantage. How many syllables do we need? And just the pure phonetics of it.” Their latest single, “pa saulei”, is written and sung in Latvian and takes the idea down to a single word. Saule is sun, pasaule is world, and pa saulei means following the sun. Moore sums up the trick: “If you add these little syllables before and after it, it can change the meaning.“ “pa saulei”, like everything they put out, never leaves the band’s hands. The four handle the engineering, mixing and visuals themselves, and for Spampinato that’s the most independent way to work: “We do everything by ourselves: recording, mixing, visuals. It’s holistic, even though I don’t like the word. It’s maybe the most independent thing you can do, just do everything.” The setting shifts every time. Their debut was made outdoors in Ērgļi, a village in Latvia, with the instruments caught as part of the surrounding soundscape. The follow-up, due in April 2027, moves indoors to Moore’s house and home studio: “We think we need that kind of closeness, but still the comfort.” The shift is deliberate: “I don’t know what the next album will be, probably in a spaceship. But every time we try to come up not only with new music, but with a new way of approaching it.“ That album, due in April 2027, will carry the material they played at Viljandi Folk, and a single built on a traditional Estonian horn melody comes first, this September. A short tour follows in November, with Helsinki confirmed for 20 November as part of the Global Club Nights series, then release concerts in April in Latvia, Estonia and, they hope, Helsinki again. For anyone hearing them for the first time, the band’s own introduction says it best: “Tell Your Birds is a four-person music collective of musicians from Latvia, Estonia and Italy. We play our original compositions with collages of Estonian, Latvian and Italian traditional folk melodies and archive recordings and texts.“     Tell Your Birds released "pa saulei" in June, with the album due in April 2027 and everything in between turning up on their Instagram       The post Interview: Tell Your Birds – Writing a Tradition for Later (September 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: Tell Your Birds 是一支由四位西贝柳斯学院成员组成的多国乐队，横跨爱沙尼亚、拉脱维亚、意大利与芬兰的音乐传统。乐队以kokle、balafon、hiiumaa kannel（弓奏Hiiu kannel）等波罗的海传统乐器为核心，叠加Spampinato的电子实时处理，将民间素材拆解重组，融入自创旋律。专辑名《Writing a Tradition for Later》暗示其创作逻辑：为尚未到来的时代写传统。制作方式延续早期森林田野录音理念——将乐器视为声音景观的一部分，让环境声与乐器声共构层次。语言上Estonian与Latvian并行使用，各人保留母语唱腔。乐队仅在集中创作期聚在一起，其余时间各自在城市生活，这种离散工作模式本身就影响其音乐的间隙感与拼贴质地。整体定位介于当代作曲、世界音乐与田野录音之间，对实验与跨界融合听众具有较高吸引力。

items.body: Learn how to pray for the pleasure of having nothing Here for you, so choose me, use me, lose me, until I die Love can make a person remarkably inventive about the terms of their own disappearance. Give everything away, call it devotion, and eventually even the damage starts looking like proof that something extraordinary is happening. On Like Moths, Italian dark synthpop project Hermidgets follows that reasoning to its terrible conclusion, with two people drawn into a relationship whose destructive potential has become part of its appeal. The single accompanies a disturbing new video and offers the fourth preview of a third album expected in early 2027. A deep, bass-heavy opening gives way to rhythmic, buzzing synthesizers, with Hermidgets’ baritone entering low and assured as the bassline and percussion settle into a thoroughly danceable groove. That persistent synth melody keeps everything moving, its abrasive edge making the tune all the more satisfying. There is something of Fad Gadget in the electronics, a trace of Brendan Perry in the voice’s sonorous gravity, and the immediate appeal of a late-1980s club hit in the way the parts fit together. The singing lends the song its weight; the rhythm makes carrying it feel almost indecently easy. The chorus lands hard on “She grants me a loaded gun,” then leaves room for the synth line to take over, its bright, wiry melody carrying a little of the peculiar magic of an old eight-bit machine. That instrumental turn is a hook in its own right, drawing the ear straight toward “I will never be the same without your deadly grace.” Hermidgets has written one of his best songs yet, catching the listener between the pleasure of an exceptionally good refrain and the awful bargain being sung. The lyrics make surrender sound increasingly devotional. “Learn how to pray for the pleasure of having nothing” imagines a point at which the loss of identity, possessions, and boundaries becomes something actively sought. The repeated invitation to be chosen, used, and discarded gives that desire an unsettling clarity. Both people remain caught in the attraction, feeding a bond they understand may consume them. By the time the moths appear, the fire has become the destination, and the promise of being wanted has swallowed any concern about what might survive. The video gives that disappearance a physical form. Shot in stark black and white against a dark background, it confines our attention to Hermidgets’ head, bare shoulders, and hands as white modeling clay obscures and distorts his features. Palms press against the face; fingers pull the material into ridges and folds; the mouth opens through a surface that seems continually on the verge of closing over it. The face becomes a succession of unstable sculptures, with black pigment introducing another disturbance late in the performance. At moments, the effort of singing seems to be the only thing keeping a recognizable person visible beneath the mass. There is a strong resemblance to Frank Tovey’s shaving-cream performances as Fad Gadget, where a familiar substance smeared across the body became an instrument of grotesque theatre. Hermidgets’ stated inspiration is French artist Olivier de Sagazan, whose transformations of the face and body provide a more direct point of reference for the clay and contorted gestures. The video concept developed independently of the song, making their eventual correspondence especially apt: the figure physically works at his own erasure while the lyrics describe an equally willing dissolution. It also extends Hermidgets’ longstanding commitment to anonymity, allowing the face to occupy the entire frame while withholding the usual reassurance of a recognizable artist. Watch the video for Like Moths below: Hermidgets is an Italian electronic project built on years of experience in the studio and onstage, with songwriting, performance, and self-produced visuals bound together by a deliberately anonymous identity. Distorted synthpop, darkwave, and intimate songwriting form the basis of the work, while the decision to keep personal biography at a distance gives listeners room to establish their own relationship with it. The debut album, The Mire, appeared in November 2020, introducing songs including This Is Over and Nothing’s Perfect. A Flaw and Perks followed in 2021, eventually joining Meaninglessness and We Tend to Disappear on the June 2024 mini-album NIHIL. For that record, Hermidgets worked with a deliberately limited setup of two analog synthesizers, drum samples, and voice, using those restrictions to concentrate the arrangements and their emotional force. The next album began to take shape publicly with Fall Apart in July 2025, followed by Sundown that December and Could I Be Better in March 2026, the latter revisiting Could Be Better from the debut. Like Moths continues that sequence with some of the project’s most immediate songwriting and most confrontational imagery. Like Moths was mixed by Matteo Sandri and mastered by Giovanni Versari. The single is out now, with Hermidgets’ third album expected in early 2027. items.body: On the cotton candy sky Written every moment of life For all eternity Wonder why we are even alive Some records come from a scene, some from a city, and some seem to come from that ugly five-minute interval after you have stared at your phone too long and suddenly hate civilization. Faded Flowers, the latest album from Turkish Darkwave duo Ductape, belongs to the third category. It looks around at modern life: crowded rooms, digital selves, obedient routines, private disintegration, and finds a species that has become astonishingly good at maintaining appearances while quietly running itself into the ground. Çağla Güleray and Furkan Güleray formed Ductape in 2019 in Istanbul, where their mix of post-punk, darkwave, Turkish and English lyrics quickly carried them well beyond the usual underground boundaries. Four albums and two EPs later, they have relocated their creative base to France. Geography changes; the unease travels well. On Faded Flowers, that unease has acquired a larger target. The title gives you the central image without turning it into homework: people as flowers left too long beneath bad light, drained by repetition, expectation, isolation, and the exhausting business of becoming whatever the surrounding machinery finds acceptable. You can hear that pressure everywhere. The basslines have the cold discipline of public transport at six in the morning. Synthesizers cut through with little sympathy. Furkan’s guitar keeps finding ways to sound agitated without becoming decorative, sometimes stalking around Çağla’s voice, sometimes answering it, sometimes scraping at the walls. Çağla’s magnificent voice remains the great destabilizing force in Ductape. She can sound detached enough to frighten you, then suddenly let some exposed nerve show through before the song has time to make a ceremony of it. There is very little comfort in that delivery, which suits an album concerned with the absurdity of living among millions of people and still feeling marooned. That particular contradiction runs all through Faded Flowers. Everyone is visible now. Everyone is reachable. Everyone is encouraged to construct a public version of themselves, polish it, post it, improve it, defend it, sell it, then wake up tomorrow and do the same miserable maintenance all over again. Somewhere along the line, identity became administrative labour. Ductape sounds thoroughly fed up with the arrangement. The album keeps circling the false authorities people submit to without necessarily believing in them: social roles, digital identities, manufactured ideals, systems of power, inherited expectations, all those little invisible rules that become oppressive mostly because nobody remembers agreeing to them. There is anger in these songs, but also exhaustion, and the exhaustion may be more interesting. Rage still assumes you have energy to spare. Fine considers one dubious convenience of hitting bottom: at least you can stop pretending the view is lovely. The album’s first single follows a collapse through pain and disorientation toward an unexpected sense of ownership, as Çağla finds a place for herself inside the very circumstances that have undone her. A steady bassline and luminous synthesizers carry her weary composure, giving that uneasy acceptance room to develop. There is something wonderfully suspect about feeling comfortable down there, and the song lets the suspicion sit beside the relief. Within an album preoccupied with keeping up appearances, surrendering the performance becomes its own small freedom. The accompanying black-and-white video turns that process into a homemade alchemical experiment. Filmed at Misuc in Ankara, it casts the duo as silent-film experimenters collecting ingredients and tending a potion among curious specimens. Ductape handled the direction, styling, and production, with camera work by Mert Yalçın and editing by Çağla Güleray. Its antique laboratory makes an apt workshop for two people attempting to assemble another version of themselves. Standout track Obscure moves with a bassline so blunt and heavy it seems capable of carrying the song by itself, while Furkan Güleray’s distorted guitar keeps worrying at the edges, leaving abrasions rather than decoration. Synths hang overhead with an icy, almost antiseptic quality, giving the music the uneasy stillness of a room where something unpleasant has already been said. Çağla Güleray sings in English, her low register remarkably composed as she picks through disillusionment without dressing it up for sympathy. That restraint makes the words hit harder. Stolen light, dead idols, resentment calcified through repetition, the dull vacancy that follows years of believing in something that eventually reveals itself as another instrument of control: Obscure gathers these ideas until the song begins to feel less like despair than the slow recognition of how thoroughly faith can be exploited. There is damage here, certainly, but also the uncomfortable clarity that comes when the old explanations have finally stopped working. Its Berlin performance video brings that severity onto the stage. Directed by Altay Erlik, with cinematography by Emrah Celik and laser animation by Peter Isachenko, the clip concentrates on the duo’s physical presence, giving the song’s accusations the directness of an encounter across a crowded room. On Gölgesiz, the effort of continuing becomes almost physical. Sung in Turkish, the album’s second single carries accumulated sorrow through persistent drums and guitar figures that seem caught in the same argument with themselves. Çağla keeps her delivery measured, making fatigue audible through the weight she gives each phrase. The rhythm maintains its appointment with the next bar while the person inside it struggles to find a reason to follow. That uneasy relationship between bodily momentum and emotional depletion gives the song its force, extending the album’s concern with lives organised around obligations that have outlasted their meaning. Made during Ductape’s Latin American tour, the monochrome DIY video places Çağla against expanses of water and open space, her figure often reduced to a silhouette. Visual distortions make her outline appear unstable, as though even occupying a body has become difficult work. The images give the song’s isolation a scale that the surrounding emptiness only enlarges. Faded Flowers gains its pull from the sense that decay is something social as much as personal. The individual breaks down because the surrounding structure is already cracked. The city keeps moving. The screen keeps glowing. The machine keeps asking for another password. Somewhere inside all that, a person still has to decide who they are. Ductape leave that question open, with the bass still moving underneath it. items.body: alarm!systemen self-titled Antibody Belgian newcomer alarm!systemen’s debut LP has a range of sounds and approaches which often belies a lack of direction or aesthetic, but that’s definitely not the case here. At large, the ten tracks on offer draw from long histories of coldwave and dream pop, but eschew slavish adherence to lo-fi nostalgia for its own sake. The classic Slowdive-isms of “Goes Again” are offset by clean, if minimal modern programming, and later on album closer “Void” serves as a reminder of how that act and other shoegaze giants found new life lifting from ambient electronics at large. On the more direct side, “Kapot” juxtaposes bricked-out synthpop drum programming with excellently reverbed guitar, and the dead simple but wonderfully executed dream pop nod of “BURN” shows just how far some wistful melodies and airy production can take you when they’re done with a measure of taste and restraint. Written over the course of five years, it’s perhaps not surprising that there’s this much variety here, but alarm!systemen’s real forte is in pulling it all off well enough to refresh familiar styles and serve as an example of how younger acts drawn to these classic sounds can rework and rethink them in their own manner. alarm!systemen by alarm!systemen Zataar First Crush CRVSH While based in France, the material released by producer Zataar draws from both her Morrocan and Belgian heritage. From the latter, you funky rhythmic electronics that hearken back to the New Beat era with a healthy dose of classic body music, where the former comes through in the melodies and instrumentation that reference North African folk music. Cuts like “Ali Sawtek” lean into the blend especially well, finding a swinging groove in the bass and drum programming, while Zataar’s vocals and the track’s melody are kept low and swirling in the mix, with big string stabs cutting through the thick reverb. As a contrast, “In the Lights You Call My Name” injects polyrhythmic complexity into the drum track, its belchy resonant bassline flowing beneath rich waves of plucks and pads. The cleverness in the arrangements really comes through on “Moments in Love”, which manages transitions between deep house styled rhythm programming and sections of Chaabi folk melodies, before combining them smoothly into a hypnotic whole. Far from a gimmick, it’s a fully realized approach that recognizes the commonality and contrasts inherent in blending multiple styles and genres, and then reconciles them handily. First Crush by Zaatar The post Observer: alarm!systemen & Zataar appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由Dorothy Moskowitz与作曲家Paladino、诗人Ferrari合作完成，包含十一首歌曲，风格被描述为前卫、氛围、模态、非线性等。音乐主要由钢琴构成，辅以弦乐、木管、合成器音色和金属声响，刻意打破听众对西方和声进行的固有认知，被比作Steve Reich和Philip Glass的极简主义路线。歌词兼具诗意与当代政治性，直接触及极权主义、种族主义等议题，同时包含对死亡和宇宙位置的哲思冥想。Moskowitz的人声演绎带有世界性的疲惫与智慧，旋律如意识流般起伏，不遵循常规调性和声，而是让每个词语获得独立的重量。整体呈现出反叛歌曲传统、融合激进政治歌词与实验音乐语言的特征。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items.body: Parissior is a Spanish project founded by DJ and producer Jesu Aparicio. With “Human Control”, he releases his debut album, featuring ten tracks (although the vinyl edition contains only eight). While several EPs were released previously, this album consists entirely of new material, exploring themes such as digital identity, illusion, authenticity, and human imperfection. Musically, this translates into a very solid mix of Dark-Techno and EBM. The basslines sound menacing and pure EBM, while the kicks reveal clear Techno influences. There are also a few additional influences, such as Acid sequences, as well as some delightful old-school Techno elements that remind me of the Frankfurt scene of the 1990s. The way everything is put together sounds intelligent and, naturally, highly dancefloor-oriented. There are also some vocals worth mentioning, including a track featuring guest vocalist Jorge Tornin, although the vocals are not necessarily the most striking aspect of the album. “Human Control” is a very strong release that delivers a perfect blend of nostalgic moments and a more contemporary sound, in which Dark-Techno and EBM are inseparable and form a powerful cocktail. An album you absolutely must discover! (Rating:8½). Listen to “Eco Machines”: Eco Machines by Parissior About Parissior Parissior is the alias of Spanish DJ and producer Jesu Aparicio. He has released singles and EPs since at least 2016, including “Could I Drown In Your Desire” and “Dance To The Groove” (Spa In Disco), followed by “Let Them Dance” (Hot Digits Music, 2017) and further EPs and compilation appearances for Golden Soul Records. From “Back To Earth” (2020) onward he has worked mainly with the Espacio Cielo label, releasing further singles, EPs and compilation tracks including “Battle Cry” (2021), “Raver In The Booth” and “Full of Stars” (2023), and the Skylax release “Antennae” (2024). “Human Control” is his first full-length album.
items._cn_summary: 西班牙制作人Jesu Aparicio以Parissior之名推出的首张全长专辑，围绕数字身份、幻觉与真实性等人文议题展开创作。整体以暗黑Techno与EBM为骨架，底频线条具有强烈的EBM攻击感，鼓机部分则显露清晰的Techno血脉。Acid序列与1990年代法兰克福老派Techno元素作为点缀出现于个别段落。制作层面注重舞池功能性，编排逻辑严密，节奏与音色层次服务于身体的运动反应。人声并非主导，但Jorge Tornin参与的曲目为机械感的声音景观注入了有机的人性维度。专辑在怀旧回溯与当代俱乐部美学之间取得了平衡，两种风格不是简单叠加而是相互渗透。评论特别推荐试听'Eco Machines'一曲以快速感受作品核心气质。

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — Well John, it was my pleasure, though my answer dates four years after your thanks. Glad you enjoythis very special project.TBH, I delayed this review, because I didn't really know what to make of this album (lasting adouble LP release plus a 45RPM single) at acquisition time. Sure, the title announces that it willbe quite a program: Vertigo of Flaws: Emancipation of the Dissonance and Temperaments in IrrationalWaveforms and it doesn't lie about the sonic contents. The Diaz brothers have widened theirsoundscapes and we find some Industrial music (very early Popol Vuh and Kluster albums aren't far) to Ozric (well almost ;-))), but it's the former trend that dominates. In some ways, it feels a bitlike scrapping the bottom of the archives drawer (not sure it is the case, though), because the duoand their guest don't try to link the different bits, and there are odd stops inside the tracks'duration.As far as the Indus side, there is nothing aurally offensive (ala Throbbing Gristle), but nothingall that pleasant either and they're grouped in two packages, separated by the usual Trees Speaksoundscapes tracks. You'll still find great spoons of spices like Tangerine Dream, Cluster, early-Kraftwerk and the hypnotic "motorik" rock of Neu! or Can in the Emancipation of the Dissonance andTemperaments in Irrational Waveforms soup. Ultimately, despite a greater sonic scope, Vertigo ofFlaws is indeed flawed and overlong, and even overstays its welcome, partly because TS fail to renewitself, despite the greater spectrum presented here. Definitely not their best effort.
items._cn_summary: Trees Speak的《Vertigo of Flaws》是一张双LP加单曲的大体量专辑，Diaz兄弟拓展了声景边界，将早期Popol Vuh与Kluster式的工业质感与Ozric式的迷幻氛围熔于一炉。专辑标题暗示了对不协和音与非常规波形的解放，作品中可见Tangerine Dream的序列合成器肌理、Cluster的电子声响实验，以及Neu!与Can式的催眠节奏感。工业段落并不刺耳，而是与Trees Speak标志性的声景段落交替呈现，形成两层结构。然而评论者指出，素材之间缺乏有机的衔接逻辑，乐曲内部存在突兀的停顿，整体显得冗长且未能实现自我更新。作为一张以电子实验为骨架、融合德国前卫摇滚传统的作品，它在声音光谱的拓展上有其价值，但结构上的松散削弱了聆听体验的连贯性。
